scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Calinda originated in the Caribbean in the 1720s, brought by enslaved Africans from the Kingdom of Kongo.
It developed as a martial art and war dance involving stick-fighting, practiced notably in Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Louisiana.
French colonial migration influenced its spread and integration into Carnival traditions.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Calinda is performed during Carnival celebrations, particularly in Trinidad and Tobago, and during cultural and religious ceremonies such as Vodou events in Haiti.
It serves as both entertainment and a martial tradition, symbolizing African heritage, resistance, and community identity.
The dance and stick-fighting contests are occasions for social gathering, competition, and cultural expression.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers in Calinda wear specific costumes during stick-fighting contests, which may include embroidered coats, ruffled linen, silk stockings, and pumps, especially in historical contexts such as New Orleans.
The fights take place in gayelles—circular arenas designated for the combat dance.
Rituals and ceremonial songs precede the fights within these spaces.

scenes.title: The people
narration: No specific notable figures are named in the sources.
However, the role of the chantwell (lead vocalist) is significant in performing lavways that accompany the dance and fights.

Calinda has regional variants across the Caribbean: in Haiti, it is a combat dance linked to Vodou ceremonies; in Guadeloupe and Martinique, it is practiced under names like l'agya, damaye, and mayolé; in Barbados, a related form is called stick-licking or stick science; in Puerto Rico, a similar dance called Kokobalé is performed with Bomba music.
Calinda descends from African combat dances from the Kingdom of Kongo, brought to the Caribbean by enslaved Africans.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Calinda is sibling of Tire machèt: Afro-Caribbean martial art from Haiti with shared origins and stick-fighting techniques.
Calinda is sibling of Bajan stick-licking: Barbadian stick-fighting tradition related to Calinda.
Calinda is sibling of Capoeira: Afro-diasporic martial art and dance with combat and musical elements.
Calinda is variant of Kokobalé: Puerto Rican dance with stick-fighting performed with Bomba music.
